# Linear models in R {.unnumbered} In hour 1 you ranked scenarios by strength of evidence and arrived at the t-statistic as the ratio of estimate to standard error. Here you fit the linear model in R and read its coefficient table. The data are the same paired differences you have worked with since Session 2: the height of the cross-pollinated plant minus the height of the self-pollinated plant within each pot. ## The paired differences {#sec-data} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: inspect the paired differences** :::: ::::{.task-container} Run the code below to see the fifteen paired differences. These are the same values you used in Sessions 2 and 3. :::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} darwin_diff |> select(pair, Cross, Self, difference) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| pair| Cross| Self| difference| |----:|------:|------:|----------:| | 1| 23.500| 17.375| 6.125| | 2| 12.000| 20.375| -8.375| | 3| 21.000| 20.000| 1.000| | 4| 22.000| 20.000| 2.000| | 5| 19.125| 18.375| 0.750| | 6| 21.500| 18.625| 2.875| | 7| 22.125| 18.625| 3.500| | 8| 20.375| 15.250| 5.125| | 9| 18.250| 16.500| 1.750| | 10| 21.625| 18.000| 3.625| | 11| 23.250| 16.250| 7.000| | 12| 21.000| 18.000| 3.000| | 13| 22.125| 12.750| 9.375| | 14| 23.000| 15.500| 7.500| | 15| 12.000| 18.000| -6.000|
::: ::: ## Fit the intercept-only model {#sec-fit} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: predict the intercept** :::: ::::{.task-container} Before running any code, write down your prediction. You have computed the mean of these differences before. What value do you expect the intercept to be? :::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lsmodel1 <- lm(difference ~ 1, data = darwin_diff) ``` ::: The formula `difference ~ 1` means "fit an intercept only." The intercept is the mean of the paired differences. The coefficient table tests whether that mean differs from zero — the same question the permutation test in Session 3 answered. ## Read the coefficient table {#sec-summary} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: read the summary output** :::: ::::{.task-container} Run the code below. Compare the intercept with your prediction, then answer: 1. What does the estimate represent? 2. What does the t-value represent, and how does it relate to the ranking exercise from hour 1? 3. Is there evidence that the mean difference is not zero?
1. The estimate is the mean of the fifteen paired differences — the average advantage of cross-pollination over self-pollination within a pot. 2. The t-value is the estimate divided by its standard error. A larger absolute t-value means the estimate is further from zero in standard-error units, just as in the ranking exercise. 3. Check the p-value. If it is below 0.05, there is evidence that the mean difference is not zero, consistent with the permutation test from Session 3.
:::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Base R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(lsmodel1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = difference ~ 1, data = darwin_diff) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -10.9917 -1.2417 0.3833 3.0083 6.7583 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 2.617 1.218 2.148 0.0497 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 4.718 on 14 degrees of freedom ``` ::: ::: ## Broom ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} broom::tidy(lsmodel1, conf.int = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| conf.low| conf.high| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:| |(Intercept) | 2.616667| 1.218195| 2.147988| 0.0497029| 0.0038992| 5.229434|
::: ::: ::: ## Confidence interval from the model {#sec-ci} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: obtain and interpret the confidence interval** :::: ::::{.task-container} Run the code below. The output is a 95% confidence interval for the mean paired difference. 1. Does this interval include zero? 2. Compare it with the confidence interval you computed in Session 2. Are the values the same (or very close)?
1. If the interval does not include zero, this is consistent with the p-value being below 0.05. 2. The values should match or be very close. The linear model and the manual computation from Session 2 use the same formula: estimate ± critical value × SE.
:::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Base R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} confint(lsmodel1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) 0.003899165 5.229434 ``` ::: ::: ## Broom ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} broom::tidy(lsmodel1, conf.int = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| conf.low| conf.high| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:| |(Intercept) | 2.616667| 1.218195| 2.147988| 0.0497029| 0.0038992| 5.229434|
::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## A simple write-up From the linear model on paired differences: "Cross-pollinated maize plants were taller on average than self-pollinated plants, with a mean paired difference of 2.62 inches (95% CI: 0.004, 5.22; t(14) = 2.15, p = 0.05)." Note: the degrees of freedom are 14 (fifteen pairs minus one), not 28. Match the values to your output. ::: ## Compare with the one-sample t-test {#sec-compare-ttest} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: confirm the equivalence** :::: ::::{.task-container} Run the code below. Compare the p-value from `t.test()` with the p-value from `summary(lsmodel1)`. They should be identical. This confirms that the intercept-only linear model on paired differences is the same test as a one-sample t-test. The linear model is the more general framework. :::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(darwin_diff$difference, mu = 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` One Sample t-test data: darwin_diff$difference t = 2.148, df = 14, p-value = 0.0497 alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: 0.003899165 5.229434169 sample estimates: mean of x 2.616667 ``` ::: ::: ## Composition task: fit the unpaired model {#sec-composition} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: write an `lm()` call for the unpaired comparison** :::: ::::{.task-container} You have just fitted a model that respects the paired design: ```r lsmodel1 <- lm(difference ~ 1, data = darwin_diff) ``` Now write an `lm()` call that ignores the pairing entirely: model height as a function of pollination type, using the original `darwin` data frame. Assign the result to `lsmodel2` and run `summary()` on it.
The response is `height`, the predictor is `type`, and the data are `darwin`. The formula takes the form `response ~ predictor`.
```r lsmodel2 <- lm(height ~ type, data = darwin) summary(lsmodel2) ```
:::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: compare the two models** :::: ::::{.task-container} Look at the coefficient table for `lsmodel2`. What does the `typeSelf` coefficient estimate? Is this the same quantity as the intercept of `lsmodel1`?
The `typeSelf` coefficient estimates the difference in mean height between self-pollinated and cross-pollinated plants — the same quantity as the intercept of `lsmodel1`, but with the opposite sign (Self minus Cross rather than Cross minus Self). The absolute value is the same.
:::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Why pairing matters Darwin paired his plants by parent because genetic lineage might play a large role in natural variance in height. By computing the difference *within each pair*, the paired analysis minimises this source of variation and isolates the effect of pollination type. The unpaired analysis ignores this structure. The lesson: a model should respect the design that generated the data. ::: ## Exit ticket {#sec-exit} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: exit question** :::: ::::{.task-container} Write your answer on paper before you leave.
